analysis.one_liner: Bans internet blocking and throttling, but locks in weak federal rules and overrides stronger state net neutrality laws.
analysis.headline: Introduced days after the FCC voted to repeal the 2015 net neutrality rules, the bill drew 42 Republican sponsors and cosponsors but never received a hearing, committee vote, or floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would write two rules into law: internet providers could not block lawful content or slow down lawful traffic. But it would also lock broadband in as a lightly regulated service, bar the Federal Communications Commission from ever adopting stronger rules — such as a ban on paid fast lanes — and stop any state from passing its own net neutrality law. It was introduced five days after the FCC voted to repeal the stricter 2015 net neutrality rules, and would have made that repeal permanent by statute.
analysis.who_benefits: Broadband providers like cable and phone companies gain the most: the two rules it codifies are ones they already accepted, while the bill permanently prevents the FCC from issuing stronger rules (including any ban on paid prioritization), overrides state net neutrality laws, and makes broadband eligible for federal universal service subsidies. Consumers get a permanent federal guarantee against blocking and throttling, but on weaker terms than the 2015 rules.

how_it_helps.text: The bill permanently prohibits broadband providers from blocking lawful content, applications, services, or non-harmful devices, and from impairing or degrading lawful internet traffic.
It makes broadband internet access service eligible to receive funding from federal universal service support mechanisms.
It declares broadband an 'information service' and forbids the FCC from expanding internet openness obligations beyond the two prohibitions in the bill, by rulemaking or otherwise.
It bars every state and political subdivision from adopting, maintaining, or enforcing any law relating to internet openness obligations for broadband.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers and internet content companies bear the cost of the weaker framework: the bill contains no ban on paid prioritization, so providers could sell faster delivery to companies able to pay while everyone else's traffic is simply not degraded. It also strips states of authority to set stricter rules and blocks the FCC from ever strengthening the protections, locking in whatever this statute allows.

drawbacks.text: The bill prohibits only blocking and impairment or degradation of traffic; the CRS summary and bill text contain no ban on paid prioritization, leaving providers free to charge companies for faster delivery of content.

Enforcement runs only through case-by-case complaint adjudication, and the FCC is barred from expanding the obligations through rulemaking, so the two protections could not be updated as the market changes.
It preempts all state internet openness laws, taking policy choices that states had made — or might make — off the table.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs two real consumer protections — no blocking, no throttling — with a framework written to prevent anything stronger from ever being adopted: no fast-lane ban, no FCC rulemaking, no state action. For anyone who wanted the stronger 2015 rules restored, the bill's main effect was to make that outcome legally impossible.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Communications Subcommittee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 19, 2017 and referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, then to its Subcommittee on Communications and Technology on December 22, 2017.
No further action was ever taken; the bill never received a subcommittee or full committee markup or a floor vote, and expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

It was introduced five days after the FCC's December 14, 2017 vote to repeal the 2015 Title II net neutrality rules, and would have written the substance of that repeal — the information-service classification and preemption of state rules — into statute, shielding it from future FCC or legislative reversal.
Although Republicans controlled the House and the bill had a Republican sponsor and 41 Republican cosponsors, the Republican chairman never scheduled it for committee consideration.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, broadband providers did not get the statutory lock-in they sought: no congressional preemption of state net neutrality laws, no statute shielding the FCC's repeal, and no universal service eligibility written into law. States and supporters of stronger net neutrality rules retained room to act, though the FCC's own repeal — which the bill was meant to entrench — took effect in 2018 anyway.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Broadband providers, denied a statutory lock-in

for.name: Marsha Blackburn
for.role: U.S. Representative, TN-7; Chair, House Communications and Technology Subcommittee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it five days after the FCC voted to repeal the 2015 net neutrality rules.

for.name: Ajit Pai
for.what_they_did: Led the FCC's December 14, 2017 vote to repeal the 2015 Title II net neutrality rules, creating the policy this bill would have codified into law.

sides.party_line_note: All 42 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat supported it, and the bill died in committee in a House controlled by the sponsor's own party.

industries.note: The bill would codify their preferred regime: it bans only blocking and throttling, locks in the light-touch 'information service' classification, forbids the FCC from ever issuing stronger rules, preempts state laws, and makes broadband eligible for federal universal service subsidies. Its main effect is to entrench the providers' freedom to sell paid fast lanes and to keep stricter rules off the table permanently.

The bill drops the paid prioritization ban from the 2015 rules, so these companies could be charged for faster delivery of their traffic — a cost that large platforms can absorb but startups cannot. They keep the guarantee that their content cannot be outright blocked.
The bill preempts every state from adopting or enforcing its own net neutrality law, removing the main avenue states had pursued after the FCC repeal.
